Thursday night
Results tomorrow. At tuition Chandrika bounced up and said, "It will be fine, yaar! You always panic for nothing!" and went back to her phone. She meant well, I know. But it felt like being patted on the head. Like my worry was a silly thing to wave off. I said "yeah" and stared at the whiteboard for an hour.
Then tonight Mummy found me sitting on the stairs. She didn't say anything at first. She sat down one step below and asked, "Which paper is scaring you?"
"Physics," I said, and told her about question six.
She listened to the whole thing. Then she said, very quietly, "It will be fine. And if it isn't, we'll work it out together."
Same words as Chandrika's. Completely different. I'm going to sleep now.
- Akash

qa.a: Physics was the paper scaring Akash, especially question six.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling after Chandrika's cheerful "It will be fine"?
qa.a: Akash felt dismissed and a little hurt, as if the worry were silly, which is why the reply was just "yeah" and an hour of staring at the whiteboard.

qa.q: Why did Mummy's version of the same words work better?
qa.a: She listened first and spoke quietly, and added that they would work it out together, so the reassurance came after Akash felt taken seriously.

qa.a: Chandrika probably thought she was cheering Akash up and had no idea the quick, bright tone came across as brushing the worry aside.

I'm Jatin, and I used to think saying sorry to my little sister Kashish was the same as losing. Two years ago she borrowed my headphones without asking, and I yelled so loudly that she cried. Mummy looked at me like I was a stranger.
I didn't apologise. I did what I always did: an hour later I sent Kashish a silly dancing-cat sticker, then acted like nothing had happened at dinner. Kashish didn't eat much. She didn't come to my room for three days, and she used to come every evening.
On the third day I sat on the edge of her bed. I didn't make a speech. I just said, "I shouted at you. That was wrong. Sorry."
She said, "Okay," and handed me back my headphones, which she'd been hiding.
That short sentence worked better than a hundred stickers.

Coach's notes - Sachin, Under-17 swimming club
On Monday, after the gala, I was taking photos for the club's page. Madhuri stepped out of the frame twice. When I waved her back, she said, "Sir, I don't want photos in my swimsuit online. I'm fine with ones in my club jacket."
A couple of teammates groaned: "Come on, it's just the team picture." I told them to stop. She had said no, and that was enough.
I took one shot with everyone in jackets instead, and deleted the earlier ones that had her in the background. I thanked her after training for saying it clearly.
It made me realise we never ask. From this week, every swimmer fills in a form saying which photos they agree to, and anyone can change their answer any time. If any adult or teammate ignores a no, they tell me or the club manager straight away.

In Class 9 our group had one week to make a video on water saving. Hansa was editing. When she showed the first cut, it was a mess: music too loud, the interview cut off halfway.
I said, "Hansa, you're useless at this. Give it to someone else." In front of everyone.
She went very quiet and closed the laptop. For two days she didn't reply in the group.
I felt bad, but I also still thought the video was bad. Both were true. What I hadn't worked out was how to say the second without saying the first.
On the third day I tried again. "The music drowns out the interview, and it stops mid-sentence at 1:20. Can we fix those two bits?"
Hansa opened the laptop. "The music is easy. Show me where at 1:20."
We finished it together that night. It was the best one in class.
- Sahil

The morning bus from Nandgaon to the town college never stopped at Mahima's village anymore. It slowed, the driver waved, and it went on, full.
For a week Mahima refused to talk at home. She sighed loudly at dinner and left her plate half full. Her friend Irawati said, "Sulking won't fix the bus."

Irawati's uncle, the sarpanch's clerk, helped them get it stamped. On Monday twenty girls and boys stood quietly at the bus stop with a banner: "Please stop for us too."
The depot sent a man to count. By the next month, one extra bus stopped at the village at seven-fifteen.
Mahima ate a full plate that night.

During the practice match, Uday was fouled hard for the second time and the other boy laughed. Uday went red and stepped right up to him, fists closed, voice rising. Two others started shouting too.

I told him walking away took more strength than shoving.

Aparna posted a thirty-second dance video on a Thursday night. By morning there were two comments that looked almost the same.
One was from Ganga, her friend since Class 3: "potato legs strike again 🥔😂". The other was from an account with no photo, created that week: "can't even move lol. delete this."

The second account had also commented on two other girls' videos from her school, each time with a laugh and "delete this." Plenty of people had liked those comments.
Aparna didn't reply. She took screenshots of all three, blocked the account, and showed her mother, who helped her report it. Then she replied to Ganga: "potato legs forever."
